title: The formal-occupancy test also limits the rule: informal positions like volunteer moderator do not count
content:
The Scenario at A.1.5.5.0.4.1.1.4 is the mirror image of the strict cases. An entity is a volunteer moderator for Sky's Discord and, without leaving that position, becomes an active Aligned Delegate. The Finding is **Aligned**, with the reasoning stated flatly: "'Volunteer Discord moderator' is not a role that is formally defined in the Atlas. Therefore, Entity's first position as volunteer Discord moderator does not count as an ecosystem role. The Target Document is not triggered at all in this Scenario."

This is what makes the bright-line rule genuinely a line rather than a general-purpose conflict-of-interest doctrine. The same test that catches an unpaid, on-call, or on-leave Atlas role lets through an unpaid position with real influence over ecosystem discourse — moderation controls who speaks and what remains visible, which is not obviously less consequential than an unranked delegateship.

The consistency is principled: the rule regulates *the Atlas's own role structure*, on the theory that roles the Atlas defines are the ones whose mandates and inner incentives it can characterize and therefore reason about. Informal positions have no defined mandate to conflict with.

But the exposure is real, and it points somewhere specific: the enforceable perimeter of the single-role rule is exactly as wide as the Atlas's role vocabulary. Any function that matters but has not been formalized sits outside it — and formalizing a role brings it inside, which means every act of formalization tightens the constraint on people already holding those positions. NR-2 and NR-3 circle nearby questions about how wide the ban should reach, but this asymmetry (formalized versus merely influential) is not among them.
description: A.1.5.5.0.4.1.1.4 finds an Aligned Delegate who is also a volunteer Discord moderator Aligned, because that position is not formally defined in the Atlas
